newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia bill sees 108 trln rbl '97 spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: Russia bill sees 108 trln rbl '97 spending cuts.

text.p: A Russian government bill to be submitted to the State Duma lower house of parliament sees 1997 spending cuts of 108 trillion roubles from the original spending plan of 530 trillion, Interfax news agency quoted First Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Petrov as saying on Monday.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin signed an order on Wednesday submitting the so-called sequester bill cutting spending to the Duma.
Petrov, in charge of the budget cut plan, said Chernomyrdin himself was likely to formally present the plan to the communist-dominated Duma.
"By all accounts, Viktor Chernomyrdin himself will present the document in the Duma on May 21," he said.

Duma budget committee head Mikhail Zadornov told Reuters the bill divided the budget into three areas -- those which would not face any cuts, those with cuts of 30 percent and those with cuts of 55 percent.

Zadornov said the communists and their allies might respond to the spending cuts bill with a bill to print money, a recourse which has been rejected by President Boris Yeltsin and top government officials.

"I do not rule out that the left part of the Duma (dominated by communists) will not offer a bill on printing money in response to the sequester bill," he said. "I know such bills are being prepared."

Finance Minister Anatoly Chubais has said the sequester bill will not affect actual spending, since it had already been slashed. First quarter outlays were 63 percent of planned levels on income of 57 percent, he said.
Zadornov said he had received the sequester bill from the government but had not received supporting documents and was unable to confirm the sum of projected spending cuts.
The budget committee may take up the bill on May 13 or 14, he said.
He said cuts of 55 percent were proposed levied on outlays to agriculture, some investment programmes, culture, health and some other social programmes.

The government proposed cuts of 30 percent on subsidies to the coal industry, delivering supplies to the icy north of Russia, and outlays for buying military equipment and supporting closed cities such as military research zones.

He said the bill did not see cuts on so-called protected areas of the budget, primarily social spending, and a few other areas including funds for natural disaster relief and allocated under Commonwealth of Independent States agreements.
But Zadornov said the government suggested stripping protected status for some educational and investment-related outlays.
Teachers' pay and some other areas would remain protected under the bill.

The investment programme known as the budget of growth would be modified to protect outlays in connection with foreign investment but would shrink to 8-10 trillion roubles from over 20 trillion, Zadornov said.
